About a week ago I was hiking with my family when my mum went to the bathroom and let out a visceral, horror movie scream. Something I've never heard in my entire life.

I didn't have time to think. Purely out of reflex, my body sprinted towards her. My dad reacted the same way. There was no thought, no bravery, no decision. We were completely unable to do anything other than run to her.

There was no real danger. A frog had simply jumped on her while she was on the toilet.

But I've been pondering it ever since, because I think it answered a prayer.

A few weeks earlier, I had been thinking about how much pain Jesus took. Betrayal, torture, humiliation, then a prolonged agony ending in death. Hours of some of the most brutal pain in history, in front of his own mother and loved ones.

And Jesus said that at any time he could have called on legions of angels to save him. He didn't. I couldn't understand that. How can anyone go through such agony, with a way out, and not take it? Does he really love us that much?

So I started praying to understand his pain. I was too scared to ask for that outright, so I hedged. I asked for 0.1% of it, or whatever he knows I can handle. Then I spent my travels on edge, waiting. Would I get stung by a rockfish while diving, bitten by a snake, tear a ligament on a hike?

I was looking for the wrong answer. I think God looked at my heart posture when I prayed. I didn't need to feel physical pain, because what I sought was to understand his nature a little better. To understand how his love transcends pain to the point of enabling the miracle of the cross.

When my mother screamed as if a tiger was attacking her, I couldn't have, in any timeline, reacted any other way than to rush to her. I can't logically explain it other than as a reflex of love, which perhaps is God's nature showing through me, and through my father, in that instant.

It sounds a bit dramatic given the frog. But that was a one-second glimpse, with no time to think. Jesus had hours, with every chance to reconsider.

He is eternal, and his nature doesn't change. If Jesus and the Father are one, then that explains the cross. He is love, and love transcends all other options. So even with the way out in front of him, he loved us, and he would never forsake us.

LONG POST

I believe this crypto bear market will be fundamentally different from anything we've experienced before.

And there's a reason for that.

For the first time in crypto's history, we're facing something that didn't exist during previous cycles: **a massive technological revolution competing for the same capital and attention.**

Artificial intelligence and quantum computing are attracting enormous amounts of investment, talent, and speculation.

In previous cycles, crypto was one of the main destinations for investors looking to gain exposure to disruptive technology.

Today, that capital has alternatives.

And whether people want to admit it or not, that changes everything.

But there's another problem, and I think it's even more important.

Crypto is running out of narratives.

Think about it.

We've gone through ICOs, DeFi, NFTs, the metaverse, GameFi, countless Layer 1s, Layer 2s, memecoins, and endless promises of mass adoption.

Every cycle introduced a new narrative, attracted fresh liquidity, created enormous speculation, and eventually left thousands of investors holding worthless tokens.

The industry has become incredibly efficient at generating hype, but far less successful at delivering sustainable value.

And eventually, people get tired.

They get tired of losing money.

They get tired of watching insiders and early investors dump on retail.

They get tired of hearing that the next revolutionary project will change the world, only to watch it collapse 90% a year later.

Crypto doesn't just have a liquidity problem. It has a credibility problem.

And I believe we're reaching a point of genuine narrative exhaustion.

Now combine all of this:

Capital and attention being diverted toward other technological sectors, declining retail enthusiasm, damaged investor confidence, and an industry saturated with projects that have little reason to exist.

What happens next?

In my view, a major purge becomes increasingly likely.

Not necessarily the death of crypto, but the destruction of a significant portion of the speculative ecosystem built around it.

And this is where I think many analysts are making a mistake.

They're still approaching this market as if we're simply repeating the same four-year cycle.

A bear market, a halving, an altseason, new all-time highs, and everyone gets rich again.

But markets evolve.

Competition for capital evolves.

Investor behavior evolves.

Why should we assume crypto will keep repeating the same cycle when the environment surrounding it has fundamentally changed?

I still believe Bitcoin and a handful of established assets have a future.

In fact, I think the eventual opportunities could be extraordinary.

But I also believe the road toward those opportunities will be far more painful than most people expect.

This isn't necessarily just another cyclical correction.

It could be a structural reset of the entire industry.

And that's precisely why I've been warning that this bear market could be longer, more destructive, and psychologically harder than anything we've experienced before.

The next great opportunity may not come from finding the next 100x altcoin. It may come from surviving the collapse of thousands of them.

Hope you understand.

Nobody catches the exact bottom, and I am not trying to. What matters is the bottom area, and for me that area is 53K to 62K. Bitcoin is trading inside it right now. This week it broke the summer low of 57k and printed 55.1K early Saturday, the lowest level since September 2024, and the market went into full panic. Panic is exactly where long-term positions are built. I remain bullish on the opportunity in front of us, and the data below shows why I am buying:

Let me explain where my bottom area comes from. The bottom of the range sits just under the Realized Price at 53.7K. Think of it as the average price everyone in the market paid for their Bitcoin. Saturday's low at 55.1K came within 1.4K of it, which means the average holder is now close to break-even. In past cycles, this is where long-term investors were buying. To be fair, in every past bear market Bitcoin also broke below its Realized Price, sometimes for months, and that is where the final capitulation happened. This is the one historical pattern I disagree with this time. So far, this is the first bear market that has never closed below its Realized Price, and I believe the bottom area is right here, between 52K and 62K. The top of the range is 62K, because many people bought between 62K and 65K in recent months. They are now underwater, and when price returns to their entry, many of them sell just to get their money back. Recent buyers paid around 74K on average, so they are deep in the red and many are selling at a loss. Their coins go to patient buyers, and that is how Bitcoin moves from weak hands to strong hands. So my plan is simple: between 52K and 62K, I accumulate. The next job for the bulls is to break back above 62-65K.

Sentiment is as well at the floor. Fear & Greed Index dropped to 6 on Saturday, one point above its February low of 5. Remember what happened the last two times sentiment was this washed out this year. In February the index hit 5 at the 60K low. In June it printed 10 near 58K, and what followed was the run to 87K. Santiment shows bearish commentary dominating social media, with the bullish-to-bearish ratio down to 0.59. Which is also a strong sign of a bottom formation that is in process. Futures (Leverage)  traders are positioned the same way and  Binance funding flipped negative during Saturday's sell-off for the first time since June, which means more shorts than longs in the market, and the 60K put has become the biggest options bet on Deribit with around $900 million in open interest. When everyone is already betting on lower prices, who is left to sell?

The weekly RSI sits around 37, and to be fair, most of historic bottoms built at a weekly RSI of 25-30, and this suggests that this is yes, the bottom area, but further sell of should not be ruled out and Iam prepared with more buy orders.  Bitcoin is also trading below its 200-week moving average, which sits around 68K. Historically, Bitcoin has spent very little time below that line, and those moments belonged to bottoming phases, not tops. And look at the timing: Saturday's low came 411 days after the October 2025 all-time high, right in the time window in which past bear markets found their lows.

Same logic as producing a chair: when the market pays far less than it costs to produce, that discount does not last forever. Miner at this level has historically shown up near bottoms, not during tops.
